fixes.explanation: Egypt is right, baker. Jeroboam returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon (2 Chronicles 10:2). Solomon, David's son (1 Kings 2:12) and Israel's king, was the one he ran from. A man who ran that far doesn't come back for nothing, and I think people were about to notice.

Assyria is a long way off from this story, friend. The text says Jeroboam returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon (2 Chronicles 10:2). Solomon, David's son (1 Kings 2:12) and Israel's king, was the king he ran from. Egypt is the place to remember on this one.

Moab is a good guess if you're picking a faraway place, but it's not this one. The text says Jeroboam returned from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon (2 Chronicles 10:2). Solomon was Israel's king and David's son (1 Kings 2:12). Jeroboam's hideout was Egypt.

Right, baker. Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon during his lifetime (2 Chronicles 10:6). Solomon was David's son (1 Kings 2:12) and Israel's king before him. These men had watched the old king work up close. I'd say that's a good first phone call.

That's right, baker. Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and served him (2 Chronicles 10:8). They'd known him for years. I bet that group felt a lot more comfortable than the elders.

God is right, baker. The text says, “So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God…” (2 Chronicles 10:15). So there's more going on here than a king who wouldn't listen. That's worth sitting with for a moment.

The Philistines aren't named anywhere in this scene, baker. The text says, “So the king did not listen to the people, and indeed this turn of events was from God…” (2 Chronicles 10:15). God is the answer. The verse points to Him, not to any outside people.

Nathan was a prophet (2 Samuel 7:2), friend, but he's not the one in this verse. The text says the word was spoken “…through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.” (2 Chronicles 10:15). So the word went to Jeroboam, who is right there in this scene.

Iddo the seer (2 Chronicles 9:29) is a good guess if you like the prophet names, baker, but the text points somewhere else. It says the word was spoken “…through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.” (2 Chronicles 10:15). Jeroboam is the one who received it.

True, baker. The text says, “…but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.” (2 Chronicles 10:17). The Israelites went home, but the ones in Judah's cities still had him as king. He was still reigning.

It's True, friend. The text says, “…but Rehoboam still reigned over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.” (2 Chronicles 10:17). Israel went home, but the Israelites in Judah's cities still had Rehoboam reigning over them. He was still king there.

Yes, baker. The text says, “And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 10:18). In haste, no speeches. A few days ago this man was giving the people a harsh answer, and now he's leaving fast.

He doesn't call the elders back, friend. The text says, “And King Rehoboam mounted his chariot in haste and escaped to Jerusalem.” (2 Chronicles 10:18). He left in haste. The text shows him heading for Jerusalem, not asking anyone for more advice.
